planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed; 'Lady' was the first English lavender bred to flower reliably in its first year from seed, making it usable as a fast, uniform bedding and container lavender as well as a permanent perennial.

directions: Sow seed indoors under lights, barely covering it since light aids germination, and expect uneven sprouting over 1-3 weeks even under ideal conditions. 'Lady' won the 1994 All-America Selections award as the first lavender ever to receive the honor, prized for its ability to bloom in dense, fragrant violet-purple spikes within five to six months of sowing rather than requiring a full second season like open-pollinated English lavender. Its compact, tidy, upright habit and uniform seedling growth make it well suited to mass plantings, edging, and containers where consistent size matters. Once established, treat it like any English lavender: provide sharp drainage, full sun, and avoid overwatering, and it will persist as a hardy perennial well beyond its first flowering season in zones 5-9.

common_name: Nana Alba Dwarf White English Lavender

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; 'Nana Alba' does not come true from seed and is propagated only by semi-hardwood cuttings.

directions: Plant in full sun with excellent, sharp drainage, and avoid heavy clay or consistently damp soil that leads to root rot. 'Nana Alba' is a dwarf English lavender selection, first recorded in Perry's Hardy Plant Farm catalog in 1928, grown for its short, tidy silvery-green mounds topped with pure snow-white flower spikes in mid- to late summer, a striking contrast to the more common blue-purple lavender varieties. Its compact size makes it ideal for edging paths, white or moon gardens, and containers where a full-size lavender would overwhelm the space. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody, and site it where reflected heat from paving or gravel can help it dry out quickly after rain.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; as a sterile lavandin hybrid, 'Edelweiss' must be propagated by cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil, spacing plants generously to accommodate its broad, mounding growth. 'Edelweiss' is the standard white-flowered lavandin, a sport of the classic lavandin type bred for buds that emerge blushed pale pink before opening to pure snowy-white spikes on long, straight stems, making it one of the most popular lavenders for cut flowers, bouquets, and wedding work. Like other lavandins it inherits vigor and heat tolerance from its spike lavender parentage, blooming later in summer than English lavender with a longer, more robust flower stem well suited to drying and fresh arrangements. Shear back hard after flowering to maintain a dense, rounded shape and prevent the woody base from splitting open.

common_name: Minimus Dwarf Culinary Sage (Little Leaf Sage)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Minimus' sets little to no viable seed and is propagated vegetatively.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Minimus' is a tightly compact dwarf selection of common culinary sage, valued for its narrow, fine-textured, aromatic gray-green leaves and abundant lavender-blue, white-lined flowers in late spring. Because it produces little to no seed, it stays tidier and less weedy over time than straight species sage, and its dense mounding habit tolerates somewhat heavier soil than other sage cultivars while remaining drought-tolerant once established. Its small stature makes it well suited to rock gardens, herb garden edging, and containers where a full-size sage would sprawl. Harvest leaves as needed for cooking and shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and prevent legginess.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings of non-flowering shoots in spring in well-drained, preferably alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Country Cream' is a variegated sport that does not come true from seed.

directions: Plant in well-drained, preferably alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Country Cream' is a bushy, semi-woody culinary oregano selected for its small aromatic leaves edged in creamy white, giving it strong ornamental value as an edging or container plant alongside its usual kitchen uses. Loose sprays of tiny pink flowers appear from summer into early autumn and are attractive to pollinators. It tolerates heat and drought well once established but resents prolonged high humidity around the crown, so give it sharp drainage and good air circulation. Propagate by cuttings of non-flowering shoots in midsummer or by division in spring or fall to maintain the cream variegation, since seedlings revert to plain green.

common_name: Valerie Finnis Artemisia (Refined Silver Western Mugwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in poor to moderately fertile, dry to medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun; divide every 2-3 years to renew vigor and contain its spreading rhizomes.

directions: Plant in poor to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; named for the English plantswoman who selected it, 'Valerie Finnis' forms an upright clump of lance-shaped, deeply jagged, white-woolly silver leaves that hold their brightness through summer heat and humidity better than the older 'Silver King' selection. Erect plumes of small, dull yellow-gray flowers appear in summer but add little ornamental value, so many gardeners shear them off to keep the silver foliage effect uninterrupted. Like other running artemisias it spreads by rhizomes and benefits from division every few years or a buried root barrier to keep it in bounds in a mixed border. Its drought, deer, and rabbit tolerance make it a dependable silver foil for blues, purples, and hot colors in a sunny bed.
